---
title: "Planning"
---


Everything else in this package looks at material you already have. This
chapter is about the question you face before collecting it, which no
established QDA tool asks at all: how much will it take?

## How many segments must be double-coded?

Interobserver studies are routinely run at whatever size was convenient and
then reported with an interval far too wide to support the claim made from
it. Donner and Rotondi give the sample size at which the *lower* bound of a
one-sided interval for kappa reaches a value you name in advance. That is the
quantity a reader cares about, since nobody ever objected that agreement was
too good.

```r
qda_plan_kappa(0.8, 0.6, 0.1, raters = 2)     # 116 segments
qda_plan_kappa(0.8, 0.6, 0.1, raters = 4)     # 62
```

Three numbers go in: the kappa you expect from a pilot or the literature, the
smallest kappa you would still defend, and the prevalence of the code.
Prevalence matters more than people expect. A code applied to a tenth of the
segments needs several times the material of one applied to a third, and the
requirement is symmetric about one half, so a conservative planner takes the
value further from it.

The other direction, for when the budget already fixed the number:

```r
qda_kappa_lower(100, kappa0 = 0.7, prevalence = 0.3, raters = 4)
```

::: {.callout-note title="Reproducing the published tables"}

The default uses the exact chi-squared quantile. The tables in the paper
were computed with it rounded to 2.71, which makes eight of their
forty-eight cells one larger. Pass `critical=2.71` and you get their
table cell for cell; the test suite checks both.
:::

## How many documents to meet a theme?

```r
qda_plan_themes(0.05, instances = 1)      # 32 documents
qda_theme_power(32, 0.05)                 # about 0.8, the other way round
```

Fugard and Potts treat the waiting time as negative binomial: how long until
a theme of known prevalence has been seen the desired number of times.

::: {.callout-warning title="Whose question this is"}

The model assumes themes are present or absent, independent of one
another, and certain to surface once present. Braun and Clarke reject the
premise for reflexive thematic analysis, where themes are constructed
rather than discovered and a population prevalence is not a meaningful
quantity. Use this where those assumptions hold, and say which conception
of a theme you are working with.
:::

## Have I collected enough?

The saturation curve in [Figures](figures.qmd) shows a trend. These give you
the number that goes in the methods section.

```r
counts <- qda_new_codes(history)
qda_saturation_ratio(counts)$notation      # "6+2"
```

Guest, Namey and Chen operationalise saturation with three parameters: a base
of documents whose codes count as what is already known, a run of consecutive
later documents inspected for new codes, and the share of new information
that still counts as saturated. The result reads `"6+2"`, meaning saturation
declared at document six and confirmed over a run of two.

When it was never reached you get `NULL` and a `reason`, which is a finding
rather than a failure.

## How far from the top am I?

A curve still climbing says nothing about how much is left. Lowe and
colleagues fit the accumulation of themes to a growth model, which estimates
how many themes there are to be found:

```r
fit <- qda_saturation_index(counts, "IW")
fit$index                       # per cent of the estimated total
qda_documents_for(fit, 95)       # documents needed to reach 95 %
```

Three models are available. `IS` assumes observations are independent, `IW`
that overlap grows with what is already known, `SW` that it grows with the
number of observations. Lowe and colleagues found no single winner, so fit
all three and look at which describes your data. That they disagree is
information: a spread between their estimates of `A` tells you how much the
answer depends on the assumption.

::: {.callout-note title="Code saturation only"}

Everything here counts codes. Hennink, Kaiser and Marconi distinguish
code saturation from meaning saturation, which no algorithm can see, and
Braun and Clarke reject saturation as a criterion for reflexive thematic
analysis. Whichever number you report, say which conception it belongs
to.
:::
